<a id="bt-01"></a>
## BT-01 - Go beyond the brief, but keep it relevant

Use given descriptions as a starting point; consider added content (extra benefits, testimonials, competitor comparisons) and propose it to stakeholders, while including only information that helps users.

- **Source:** PDF 126 (printed 125), 127 (printed 126)
- **Applies when:** Product pages and marketing content.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Don't let given product descriptions or guidelines limit creativity; use them as a starting point and consider angles or content types that add value.
- Ask: are there benefits not in the brief? Could testimonials give social proof and build trust? Would a side-by-side comparison show how the product stacks up? Propose these to stakeholders even if outside the original scope.
- The corrected vacuum card adds feature-specific coloured icons and a '3X more powerful suction compared to other brands' comparison bar.
- Be creative but keep it relevant: only include information users find useful (see SIM-01's relevance test).

**Mistake:** Settling for 'good enough' content that only restates the brief.  
**Effect:** Missed engagement and competitive edge.

**Correction:** Add value-adding content (comparison, social proof, distinctive icons) that passes the relevance test.  
**Why it works:** Deeper engagement from content that answers real user questions.

**Observable checks:**
- Is there a user question (proof, comparison) the page leaves unanswered?
- Does each added element pass the SIM-01 relevance test?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- The source text contains typos ('tak', 'compare to') not relevant to the lesson.

**Related:** [SIM-01](07-simplicity.md#sim-01), [LAY-05](09-layout.md#lay-05), [IC-04](16-interaction-cost.md#ic-04)

<a id="bt-02"></a>
## BT-02 - Overlap images with background-matching outlines

Overlapping images add depth and sophistication; to keep the overlap from clashing, give overlapping images an outline that matches the background.

- **Source:** PDF 132 (printed 131), 133 (printed 132)
- **Applies when:** Cards with a cover image and a profile/product thumbnail; avatar stacks.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Overlapping images break linear monotony and feel dynamic and engaging when done correctly.
- A basic segmented layout (images separated by space) is functional and clear but lacks flair and feels uninspiring.
- Overlapping without care makes images and colours clash, creating a jarring experience.
- The fine-tuned version gives overlapping images outlines that match the background, separating each element, creating natural white space and making the overlap harmonious.

**Mistake:** Overlapping product image and avatars with no separation ring.  
**Effect:** Colours clash; elements merge.

**Correction:** Add a background-coloured ring (border) around each overlapping image.  
**Why it works:** The ring creates a gap that separates layers.

**Observable checks:**
- Do overlapping avatars or images have a border matching the surface behind them?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [CNS-03](11-consistency.md#cns-03), [DEP-01](13-depth.md#dep-01)

<a id="mob-01"></a>
## MOB-01 - Design for the thumb zone

Phones are often used one-handed; place key buttons, navigation and CTAs within easy thumb reach, since elements outside it are hard to reach and cause misclicks.

- **Source:** PDF 134 (printed 133), 135 (printed 134)
- **Applies when:** Mobile layouts.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Mobile devices are often operated with one hand, mainly the thumb; the thumb zone is the area easily reachable with the thumb.
- Place key elements (buttons, navigation links, CTAs) within the thumb zone; outside it they are hard to reach and can cause frustration or misclicks. Make the most-used features accessible there.
- A Sign In button at the top right is outside the thumb zone, so users stretch or adjust grip, especially inconvenient on the go or with limited mobility; placing CTAs at the bottom puts them where thumbs naturally rest.

**Mistake:** Primary or frequent actions at the top of the screen.  
**Effect:** Stretching, grip changes, misclicks.

**Correction:** Move key actions to the lower part of the screen (stacked bottom CTAs, bottom navigation).  
**Why it works:** Reachability lowers physical effort.

**Observable checks:**
- On mobile, are the primary and frequent actions in the lower area of the screen?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The heat-map figure shows Hard (top and bottom-right corner), Stretch (middle/upper right) and Easy (lower-left/centre); this reflects one hand position and should not be read as exact zones for all users.

**Related:** [IC-02](16-interaction-cost.md#ic-02)

<a id="sta-01"></a>
## STA-01 - Turn empty states into guidance

A bare 'You have no projects' is a dead end; a good empty state explains the value, gives actionable tips and offers a direct CTA, optionally with an illustration.

- **Source:** PDF 136 (printed 135), 137 (printed 136)
- **Applies when:** Empty lists, first-run screens, zero-result states.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- An empty screen with no guidance or next steps feels like a roadblock and leaves users lost; it's a missed opportunity.
- A well-designed empty state educates, engages and encourages action: a solution-oriented headline, an illustration that makes it less daunting, actionable tips (invite team members, set deadlines) and a CTA such as 'Create new project'.

**Mistake:** Only 'You have no projects!' on an empty screen.  
**Effect:** Users feel stuck and unsure what to do.

**Correction:** Headline with the benefit, short tips, primary CTA, optional illustration.  
**Why it works:** Converts a dead end into onboarding.

**Observable checks:**
- Does every empty state include a next action (CTA) and a sentence explaining what to do?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [STA-02](19-content-and-states.md#sta-02), [IC-10](16-interaction-cost.md#ic-10)

<a id="sta-02"></a>
## STA-02 - Make error states explain and recover

A good error state says clearly what went wrong, offers a clear, actionable fix and keeps the visual style of the rest of the product; 404 pages should include helpful links or search.

- **Source:** PDF 138 (printed 137), 139 (printed 138)
- **Applies when:** Form validation errors, 404 and other error pages.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Error states are where journeys go awry; bad ones leave users frustrated and confused about what went wrong and how to fix it.
- A good error state: 1) clearly communicates what went wrong, 2) offers a clear and actionable solution, 3) maintains a consistent visual style with the rest of the app or site.
- A bad 404 only says the page can't be found; a good 404 also provides helpful links or suggestions to get back on track.

**Mistake:** A 404 that only states the error (e.g. 'That's all we know') with no way forward.  
**Effect:** Users feel lost and leave.

**Correction:** Friendly explanation, error code, list of helpful links (Home, Search, Help…) and/or search, keeping the site header and style.  
**Why it works:** Shows the user's needs were considered even in failure.

**Observable checks:**
- Does each error message say what happened and what to do next?
- Do error pages keep site navigation and provide links or search?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [COL-04](14-color.md#col-04), [STA-03](19-content-and-states.md#sta-03), [STA-01](19-content-and-states.md#sta-01)

<a id="sta-03"></a>
## STA-03 - Blend creativity with brand identity in error pages

A 404 can show brand personality through on-brand illustrations, humorous copy or interactive elements, while still guiding users back to content.

- **Source:** PDF 140 (printed 139)
- **Applies when:** 404 and other error/empty pages.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Inject creativity and brand elements (on-brand illustrations, humorous copy, interactive elements) into error states while guiding users back; this turns frustration into a positive, memorable brand interaction.

**Mistake:** Generic, off-brand error page.  
**Effect:** Missed chance to soften the failure.

**Correction:** On-brand illustration and copy plus a recovery path (e.g. search).  
**Why it works:** Delight plus recovery leaves a positive impression.

**Observable checks:**
- Does the error page reflect the brand and still offer a way forward?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [STA-02](19-content-and-states.md#sta-02)

<a id="nav-01"></a>
## NAV-01 - Improve navigation dropdowns with icons, grouping and selective images

Icons quickly communicate each menu item's purpose; grouping items under category labels reveals structure; images add context but should be used only for items you want to highlight.

- **Source:** PDF 141 (printed 140), 142 (printed 141)
- **Applies when:** Top navigation dropdowns and mega-menus.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Including icons in dropdowns improves UX: icons are visual aids that communicate purpose or content, making the menu more attractive and usable.
- Group related items under distinct categories so users grasp the structure and find what they need.
- Images give more comprehensive context than icons, but less is more: an image next to every item overwhelms and clutters; enhance only the items you want to highlight.

**Mistake:** A text-only two-column menu without category labels.  
**Effect:** Slower to scan; structure unclear.

**Correction:** Icon per item, category headings (e.g. Products / Use cases), a 'New' badge where relevant, images only on a highlighted sub-section (e.g. latest blog posts).  
**Why it works:** Visual anchors plus structure speed finding.

**Observable checks:**
- Do mega-menu items have icons and category headings?
- Are images applied to every item (clutter) or only to highlighted ones?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Related:** [CNS-05](11-consistency.md#cns-05), [IC-04](16-interaction-cost.md#ic-04), [DEP-01](13-depth.md#dep-01)
